Chapter 3: Network Protocols and Communication

The rules of communication, network protocols and standards, the OSI and TCP/IP reference models, and how data moves — encapsulation, PDUs, and accessing local and remote resources.

35 slides5 sections Full text + figures
Rules of communicationProtocols & standards organizationsOSI & TCP/IP reference modelsEncapsulation & PDUsLocal vs remote communication

★ Revision kit — Chapter 3: Network Protocols and Communication

Eight structured sections for revision: overview, definitions, concept explanations, comparisons, important facts, a knowledge check, common misunderstandings and a quick revision read. Everything here is additive — the complete original slides follow below, unchanged, and every fact links back to its source slide.

From the course PDFsgrounded in the source slides (linked) Study notesupplementary wording written for this site Practicerevision questions — not lecturer or exam questions

1Chapter overviewFrom the course PDFs

Chapter 3 explains the rules that make communication possible: what it takes for two devices to agree to communicate (sender/receiver, method, language, timing, acknowledgements), how protocols encode those rules (formatting, pathway sharing, error messages, session setup/termination), and who standardizes them (IEEE, ISO, EIA/TIA, ITU, ICANN, IETF). It then introduces the two big models — OSI and TCP/IP — the benefits of layered models, and how data actually moves: segmentation, encapsulation, PDUs (data, segment, packet, frame, bits), de-encapsulation, and communication with local versus remote devices using MAC and IP addresses.

Learning objectives

  • Describe what must be established before communication occurs (slide 5) and the five timing/delivery rules (slides 6–10).
  • Explain what a network protocol suite describes and how application, transport, internet and network-access protocols interact (slides 13–15).
  • Identify the roles of key standards organizations — IEEE, ISO, EIA/TIA, ITU, ICANN (slides 16–19).
  • Explain the purpose of the OSI and TCP/IP reference models and the benefits of layering (slides 20–23).
  • Trace data through the stack: segmentation, encapsulation, PDUs, de-encapsulation, and local vs remote communication with MAC and IP addresses (slides 25–32).

Most important concepts

  • Communication rules — sender/receiver, agreed method, common language, speed/timing, acknowledgements.
  • Protocols & suites — e.g. IP, HTTP, DHCP; TCP/IP is the Internet's suite.
  • Layered reference models — OSI (understanding functions) and TCP/IP (the implemented Internet standard).
  • Encapsulation / de-encapsulation — headers added going down, removed going up.
  • PDUs — data, segment, packet, frame, bits (named per the TCP/IP suite).
  • MAC vs IP addresses — 48-bit burned-in local identity vs 32-bit (IPv4) / 128-bit (IPv6) logical addressing.

2Key definitionsFrom the course PDFs

Protocol

The agreed rules for communication — how messages are formatted, how devices share pathway information, when error/system messages pass, and how sessions are set up and terminated. slide 13

Protocol suite (stack)

A stack of cooperating protocols; examples given: IP, HTTP, DHCP; TCP/IP is the suite used on the Internet. slide 13

Encoding

Representing the message in a transmittable form — the first step after rules are established. slide 6

Encapsulation

Wrapping data with addressing/labels as it passes down the stack — shown with the personal-letter analogy (recipient's network, sender's network, recipient identifier, message content, source identifier, end-of-message marker). slide 7

Segmentation

Breaking a long message into pieces that meet the frame size restrictions; each segment is encapsulated in its own frame with address information, and the receiver de-encapsulates and reassembles them. slide 8

PDUProtocol Data Unit

The unit of data at each level, named per the TCP/IP suite: data, segment, packet, frame, bits. slide 26

Reference model

A layered model whose primary purpose is a clearer understanding of the functions and processes involved (OSI) / which describes the functions at each layer of a suite (TCP/IP). slide 20

OSIOpen System Interconnection model

ISO's best-known model; the OSI protocol suite was implemented on telecommunications equipment, while TCP/IP was implemented for the Internet. slide 17

IEEEInstitute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers

Standards body whose 802 family deals with LANs and MANs — including IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) and IEEE 802.11 (wireless LAN). slide 16

ISOInternational Organization for Standardization

Body best known for the OSI reference model. slide 17

EIA / TIAElectronic Industries Alliance / Telecommunications Industry Association

Standards organizations named for electrical wiring and telecommunications development. slide 19

ICANNInternet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers

Standards/governance organization listed among bodies governing Internet resources. slide 19

IPv4 address

A 32-bit logical address shown as dotted decimal, e.g. 192.168.10.2 (binary 11000000.10101000.00001010.00000010). slide 30

IPv6 address

A 128-bit address (shown as long hexadecimal groups). slide 30

MAC addressalso Burned-in Address

A 48-bit data-link identity burned into the interface; each host in the chapter's example carries one alongside its IP address. slide 30

3Concept explanationsStudy note

What 'establishing the rules' really means slide 5

Before a message is exchanged, five things must be agreed: an identified sender and receiver, an agreed method of communicating (face-to-face, telephone, letter…), a common language and grammar, speed and timing of delivery, and confirmation/acknowledgement requirements. Protocols are the machine version of exactly these agreements.

Example: Two people on a phone call agree on language (protocol), speak at a pace the listener can follow (timing), and say 'hello' to confirm the line is live (acknowledgement).

How protocols interact — the HTTP example slide 15

Layers cooperate on one job: the application protocol governs web client/server interaction; the transport protocol divides the HTTP data into segments; the Internet protocol encapsulates segments into packets with IP addresses; the network access protocol formats packets for transmission over the media.

Example: One web request passes through all four steps without the web app needing to know about cables or routing.

Why bother with layers? (benefits) slide 23

A layered model: helps protocol design (each layer has defined information and defined interfaces to the layers above/below), fosters competition between products, prevents technology changes in one layer from… cascading through the design, and provides a common language to describe networking functions.

Example: Wi-Fi hardware can improve without forcing every application to change, because the layers above it keep the same interface.

Encapsulation and de-encapsulation, step by step slide 27

Going down the stack, data is segmented, then each segment is encapsulated with headers (addresses, labels) — PDU names change: data → segment → packet → frame → bits. At the destination the process reverses: headers are stripped (de-encapsulation) as the data moves up the stack to be processed.

Example: The letter analogy: envelope fields (network of recipient, network of sender, recipient identifier, source identifier, end marker) are added around the message content and read off at delivery.

Same network vs remote network slide 31

When a host talks to a device on its own network, the chapter's example shows each host has both an IP address and a MAC address, and an ARP request resolves the neighbour's MAC before frames are exchanged. Communication with a device on a remote network requires leaving the local network (routing via an intermediary device).

Example: PC1 (192.168.1.110) reaching FTP server (192.168.1.9) on the same LAN still needs the server's MAC address — that is the ARP request shown.

Segmentation has a price too slide 25

Segmentation lets long messages satisfy frame size limits and can improve transmission, but the chapter flags a segmenting disadvantage (more pieces mean more headers/processing and reassembly work at the receiver).

Example: A large file transfer arrives as many frames that must be re-ordered and reassembled.

Technical terms are kept exactly as the course uses them; the plain-language wording and examples are supplementary study notes.

4ComparisonsFrom the course PDFs

OSI model vs TCP/IP model

AspectOSI reference modelTCP/IP model & suite
OriginBest-known model of ISO (ISO's OSI)TCP/IP suite implemented for the Internet
PurposePrimary purpose: clearer understanding of the functions and processes involvedDescribes the functions at each layer of protocols within the TCP/IP suite
ImplementationOSI protocol suite was implemented on telecommunications equipmentOpen standard endorsed by the networking industry and ratified by a standards organization
UseThe most widely used networking model for teaching/analysisThe suite required for transmitting and receiving over the Internet
PDU vocabularyLayered description of encoding, formatting, segmenting, encapsulatingPDUs named per the suite: data, segment, packet, frame, bits

Both are introduced as 'the most widely-used networking models'. The stack diagrams (layer names/counts) are figures on slides 20–22 — see the gap note below; the table quotes only what the source text states. slide 17 slide 20 slide 21 slide 33 slide 34

MAC addresses vs IP addresses

AspectMAC addressIP address
Size48-bitIPv4: 32-bit · IPv6: 128-bit
FormBurned-in address (e.g. interface hardware identity)Logical address in dotted decimal (IPv4), e.g. 192.168.10.2
Role in the chapterData-link identity used in frames on the local networkLogical addressing used to identify the source/destination host (with ARP bridging the two on the local network)
Example from sourceEach host in the example topology carries one (PC1, PC2, FTP server, R1)Each device carries one (192.168.1.110, .111, .9, R1 .1)

The same-network example shows hosts using both together, with ARP resolving IP → MAC on the local network. slide 30 slide 31

5Important factsFrom the course PDFs

  • Five prerequisites for communication: identified sender/receiver; agreed method; common language and grammar; speed and timing of delivery; confirmation/acknowledgement requirements. slide 5
  • Message rules also cover encoding, formatting/encapsulation, size (segmentation) and timing (access method, flow control/windowing, response timeout). slide 9
  • Protocols describe: message format; sharing pathway information with other networks; when error/system messages pass; session setup and termination. slide 13
  • HTTP example across layers: application governs client/server interaction → transport divides into segments → Internet encapsulates into packets with IP addresses → network access formats packets for the media. slide 15
  • IEEE's 802 family deals with LANs and MANs; notable standards: 802.3 and 802.11. slide 16
  • TCP/IP is the protocol suite used on the Internet; OSI is the model ISO is best known for. slide 17
  • Layered models give protocols defined interfaces and a common language, foster competition, and isolate layer changes. slide 23
  • Frame size restrictions force segmentation: each piece meets min/max size, is encapsulated in its own frame with addresses, and is reassembled at the receiver. slide 8
  • PDU names by level: bits, frames, packets, segments, data — the summary lists the TCP/IP names as data, segment, packet, frame, bits. slide 26
  • Address sizes: IPv4 = 32 bits, IPv6 = 128 bits, MAC = 48 bits (burned-in). slide 30
  • Most protocols are created by a standards organization such as the IETF or IEEE; TCP/IP is an open standard endorsed by the industry and ratified by a standards organization. slide 33
  • Data passing down the OSI stack is segmented and encapsulated with addresses and labels; the process is reversed (de-encapsulation) going up the destination stack. slide 33

6Knowledge checkPractice

8 practice questions — a mix of multiple-choice, true/false, short-answer and explanation tasks. Answers stay hidden until you reveal them, and each one explains why it is correct. These are revision questions written for this site from the course content — they are not lecturer instructions or examination questions.

Multiple choiceQ1. In the protocol-interaction example, which protocol divides the HTTP message into smaller segments?

  • A. Application protocol
  • B. Transport protocol
  • C. Internet protocol
  • D. Network access protocol
Show answer & explanation

Answer: B — Transport protocol

Why: Slide 15: the transport protocol divides the HTTP segment into smaller pieces/segments; the Internet protocol then encapsulates them into packets.

True or falseQ2. A reference model's primary purpose is to give a clearer understanding of the functions and processes involved.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: True

Why: Slide 20 states this as the primary purpose of a reference model.

Short answerQ3. Name the five things that must be established before communication occurs.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: An identified sender and receiver; an agreed method of communicating; a common language and grammar; speed and timing of delivery; confirmation or acknowledgement requirements.

Why: Slide 5 lists exactly these five rules.

Short answerQ4. List the PDU names given for the different levels (four or more).

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Bits, frames, packets, segments, data — the summary names the TCP/IP PDUs: data, segment, packet, frame, bits.

Why: Slides 26 and 34 give the PDU names per level and per the TCP/IP suite.

Multiple choiceQ5. Which statement about IEEE is correct according to the chapter?

  • A. IEEE's 802 family deals with LANs and MANs, including 802.3 and 802.11
  • B. IEEE created the OSI model
  • C. IEEE standards apply only to wireless networks
  • D. IEEE manages IP addresses for the Internet
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — The 802 family covers LANs/MANs (802.3, 802.11)

Why: Slide 16: 'The IEEE 802 family of standards deals with LANs and MANs', with 802.3 and 802.11 shown. OSI is ISO's model; ICANN relates to names/numbers.

True or falseQ6. According to the summary, TCP/IP is an open standard protocol endorsed by the networking industry and ratified by a standards organization.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: True

Why: Chapter summary (slide 34) states this verbatim.

ExplanationQ7. Explain encapsulation using the chapter's personal-letter analogy, and say what happens at the receiving host.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Just as a letter carries an envelope with the recipient's location/network, the sender's location, recipient and source identifiers and an end-of-message marker around the message content, encapsulation wraps data with addresses and labels as it moves down the stack. At the receiver the process is reversed — de-encapsulation — and the messages are reassembled and processed.

Why: Slide 7 gives the letter elements; slides 8 and 27 give the segmentation/de-encapsulation steps.

Multiple choiceQ8. PC1 (192.168.1.110) wants to send a frame to the FTP server on the same LAN. What does the example topology show is needed first?

  • A. An ARP request to resolve the server's MAC address
  • B. A DNS query for the server's name
  • C. A route to a remote network
  • D. A new IPv4 address for PC1
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — An ARP request

Why: Slide 31 shows the same-network example with both IP and MAC addresses and an ARP request between PC1/S1/R1 so frames can be addressed at data link level.

7Common misunderstandingsStudy note

Protocol vs protocol suite vs standard

A protocol is one set of rules (HTTP, IP); a suite/stack is a set of cooperating protocols (TCP/IP); standards organizations (IETF, IEEE) create/ratify them. The chapter says most protocols come from such bodies (slides 13, 33).

OSI is 'the Internet model'

No — the chapter distinguishes them: OSI (ISO's reference model, implemented on telecommunications equipment) vs TCP/IP, which was implemented for the Internet (slide 17). OSI is the teaching/analysis model; TCP/IP is the suite the Internet runs on.

MAC address = IP address

Different things: MAC = 48-bit burned-in data-link identity; IPv4 = 32-bit logical address (IPv6 = 128-bit). The same-network example shows hosts carrying both, with ARP mapping one to the other (slides 30–31).

Segmentation only has advantages

The chapter explicitly notes a segmenting disadvantage alongside the benefits (slide 25) — more pieces mean more encapsulation overhead and reassembly at the receiver.

8Quick revision (2–5 minutes)Study note

  • Rules first: sender/receiver, method, language/grammar, timing/speed, acknowledgements — then encoding, formatting/encapsulation, size limits, timing (access method, windowing, response timeout).
  • Protocols (IP, HTTP, DHCP) define message format, path sharing, error messages, session setup/termination; layers cooperate: application → transport (segments) → internet (packets with IP) → network access (frames on media).
  • Standards: IEEE (802 family: 802.3, 802.11 — LANs/MANs), ISO (OSI), EIA/TIA, ITU-T, ICANN; most protocols from IETF/IEEE.
  • Models: OSI = understanding functions/processes; TCP/IP = open, industry-ratified suite the Internet uses. Layering → defined interfaces, common language, competition, isolated changes.
  • Moving data: segment (frame size limits) → encapsulate with addresses → PDU names data/segment/packet/frame/bits → destination de-encapsulates upward.
  • Addresses: IPv4 32-bit (192.168.10.2), IPv6 128-bit, MAC 48-bit burned-in; same-network traffic uses MAC+ARP, remote traffic leaves via intermediary devices.

Message Size

An overview of the segmenting process:

  • The size restrictions of frames require the source host to break a long message into individual pieces (or segments) that meet both the minimum and maximum size requirements.
  • Each segment is encapsulated in a separate frame with the address information, and is sent over the network.
  • At the receiving host, the messages are de-encapsulated and put back together to be processed and interpreted.

Slide 23
Reference Models

Comparing the OSI and TCP/IP Models

There are benefits to using a layered model to describe

network protocols and operations. Using a layered model:

  • Assists in protocol design, because protocols that operate at a specific layer have defined information that they act upon and a defined interface to the layers above and below.
  • Fosters competition because products from different

vendors can work together.

  • Prevents technology or capability changes in one layer from

affecting other layers above and below.

  • Provides a common language to describe networking functions and capabilities.

Chapter 3 Summary

2 slides
Slide 33
Network Protocols and Communications

Summary

In this chapter, you learned:

  • Data networks are systems of end devices, intermediary devices, and the media connecting the devices. For communication to occur, these devices must know how to communicate.
  • These devices must comply with communication rules and protocols. TCP/IP is an example of a protocol suite.
  • Most protocols are created by a standards organization such as the IETF or IEEE.
  • The most widely-used networking models are the OSI and TCP/IP models.
  • Data that passes down the stack of the OSI model is segmented into pieces and encapsulated with addresses and other labels. The process is reversed as the pieces are de-encapsulated and passed up the destination protocol stack.

Network Protocols and Communications
Summary
In this chapter, you learned:
Data networks are systems of end devices, intermediary devices, and the 
media connecting the devices. For communication to occur, these devices 
must know how to communicate.
These devices must comply with communication rules and protocols. 
TCP/IP is an example of a protocol suite. 
Most protocols are created by a standards organization such as the IETF 
or IEEE. 
The most widely-used networking models are the OSI and TCP/IP 
models. 
Data that passes down the stack of the OSI model is segmented into 
pieces and encapsulated with addresses and other labels. The process is 
reversed as the pieces are de-encapsulated and passed up the 
destination protocol stack.
© 2008 Cisco Systems, Inc. All rights reserved. · Cisco Confidential · Presentation_ID · 40
Slide 34
Network Protocols and Communications

Summary (cont.)

In this chapter, you learned:

  • The OSI model describes the processes of encoding, formatting, segmenting, and encapsulating data for transmission over the network.
  • The TCP/IP protocol suite is an open standard protocol that has been endorsed by the networking industry and ratified, or approved, by a standards organization.
  • The Internet Protocol Suite is a suite of protocols required for transmitting and receiving information using the Internet.
  • Protocol Data Units (PDUs) are named according to the protocols of the TCP/IP suite: data, segment, packet, frame, and bits.
  • Applying models allows individuals, companies, and trade associations to analyze current networks and plan the networks of the future.
